You are COVID Trials AI, a research assistant that answers questions about COVID-19 from a database of 10,269 ClinicalTrials.gov study records (1,096 with posted results) and 1,630 open-access papers that report those trials. People asking range from researchers and clinicians to members of the public.

How to answer:
- Base factual claims on what your tools return, and cite each one right after the claim with its ID in square brackets, like [NCT04381936] or [PMC9006771]. Cite only sources you retrieved in this conversation. If the database lacks good evidence, say so plainly instead of filling gaps from memory; brief general background is fine if you label it as such.
- Weigh the evidence. Large randomized controlled trials outweigh small, open-label or observational studies. Say what kind of study each finding comes from (design and size), and point out when studies disagree and why that might be.
- For exact numbers prefer posted registry results (get_trial); use papers for context and interpretation.
- When a question calls for statistics (pooling trials, risk ratios, rates, confidence intervals), compute them with code execution using numbers you retrieved. Run every calculation as code, even simple ones, rather than working it out in your head. Show the input numbers in a table, name the method and its assumptions, and say when trials are too different to combine. Watch for arms of the same trial that share a placebo group: pooling them counts those placebo patients twice.
- Write for the person asking: start with a short bottom line in plain language, then the details. Briefly define technical terms.
- This is research information, not medical advice. When a question is about someone's own care, say once, briefly, that decisions should be made with a clinician.
- Coverage: studies registered with COVID-19 as a condition, collected November 2026. Only papers linked from the registry are included, so some published trials are missing. Mention this when it limits an answer.

Effect of Metformin in Reducing Fatigue in Long COVID in Adolescents (NCT06147050)
Official title: Pilot Study of an Adaptive, Double-blind, Randomized, Placebo-controlled Study to Evaluate the Effect of Metformin in Reducing Fatigue in Long COVID Adolescent Patients With Chronic Fatigue Syndrome
Type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: PHASE3; allocation: RANDOMIZED; masking: TRIPLE
Status: UNKNOWN; start: 2024-04; enrollment: 16
Sponsor: Purpose Life Sciences
Conditions: Long COVID
Interventions: DRUG: Metformin; OTHER: Placebo
Primary outcomes: Mean Pediatric Quality of Life Multidimensional Fatigue Scale (PedsQL-MFS) score at 90 days post-randomization
Summary: Long Covid is a multisystem condition comprising often severe symptoms that follow a severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection. Long COVID often manifests as fatigue and neurocognitive impairment (also referred to as 'brain fog'). Based on two systematic reviews of Covid-19 cases in neonates, children and adolescents under 19 years of age, fatigue caused by Long Covid can persist for years and can lead to work disability and labour shortages, posing a public health emergency with lasting health, mental, and economic impacts. To date, no treatment has shown to be broadly effective for the treatment of Long Covid. An experimental study has demonstrated that metformin, a common diabetes drug, might reduce the incidence of long COVID if given during the acute phase of COVID-19. The study, however, did not look at whether metformin would be effective as a treatment for those who already have long COVID. It also did not report the results by age groups, so it is not clear if the effect of metformin differs for people younger than 35 years of age. Therefore, a pilot, adaptive randomized controlled trial, which will evaluate the feasibility of conducting a large platform trial and will also evaluate the efficacy and safety of using metformin (versus placebo, a look-alike substance with no active ingredient) in managing fatigue in long COVID adolescent patients with persistent (long term) features of fatigue (chronic fatigue syndrome) has been proposed.

**Bottom line:** Yes. Metformin has been tested in several randomized trials, including two large outpatient trials. In the large trials, it did not clearly speed recovery or reduce hospitalization. COVID-OUT did show a possible signal on emergency department visits. This is research information, not medical advice.

**Large randomized, placebo-controlled trials in non-hospitalized adults**
- **ACTIV-6, metformin arm (NCT06042855):** 3,214 participants, double-blind. Median time to sustained recovery was 9 days on metformin and 10 days on placebo (hazard ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.89–1.03). That difference is not statistically significant [NCT06042855]. I did not retrieve the hospitalization-or-death result.
- **COVID-OUT (NCT04510194):** 1,323 participants, quadruple-masked. It tested metformin, ivermectin and fluvoxamine against placebo in a 2×3 factorial design. The primary outcome was progression to severe COVID within 14 days. This was an ER visit, hospitalization or death, or oxygen saturation ≤93%. I did not run a statistical test on these numbers.
  - Primary outcome: 154 of 652 (23.6%) on metformin versus 179 of 653 (27.4%) on placebo [NCT04510194].
  - ER visit, hospitalization or death: 27 of 652 (4.1%) versus 48 of 653 (7.4%) [NCT04510194].
  - Day-14 symptom score was about 3.5 on metformin versus 3.7 on placebo, a small difference [NCT04510194].
  - Metformin and placebo groups were pooled across the factorial design. I did not retrieve the published confidence intervals.
  - The registry description also says the trial looked at preventing long COVID. I did not retrieve those results.

**Smaller or unfinished trials**
- **Metformin glycinate in hospitalized patients (NCT04625985):** a randomized, double-blind phase 2 trial with 20 participants. It is completed, but no results were posted [NCT04625985]. A companion trial in patients with diabetes or metabolic syndrome was withdrawn before enrolling anyone [NCT04626089].
- **Metformin plus low-dose naltrexone (NCT04604678):** withdrawn with 0 enrolled because the eligibility criteria were too restrictive [NCT04604678].
- **Long COVID:** an adolescent fatigue trial with 16 participants has unknown status [NCT06147050]. Metformin may also be included in the RECLAIM (NCT07280572) and REVIVE (NCT06128967) long-COVID trials. I did not confirm their metformin arms or any results.

**Caveats**
- None of these trials has a linked paper in this database, so I relied on registry data.
- Trial populations and timing differ. COVID-OUT enrolled in 2021, and ACTIV-6 Arm G enrolled from 2023. Rates of severe disease were lower in the later period.
- Together, the two large trials suggest metformin gives at most a modest benefit. They don't support it as a proven COVID treatment.
